The researchers conducted the first comprehensive evaluation of emerging materials and manufacturing technologies to enable fully non-metallic gas turbine engines.
Fused deposition modeling (FDM) was used to fabricate polymer matrix composite components, with a focus on reducing porosity and optimizing mechanical properties.
Binder jet printing was adapted to fabricate ceramic matrix composite components, with challenges in achieving high density and incorporating chopped fiber reinforcement.
The non-metallic engine design was estimated to reduce engine weight by 15%, fuel burn by 4.9%, and NOx emissions by 8.3% compared to a baseline regional jet engine.
The fused deposition modeling process for polymer matrix composites was at TRL 4, while the binder jet process for ceramic matrix composites was at TRL 3.
Next steps include further optimization of the additive manufacturing processes, such as using spherical SiC powders, exploring alternate densification approaches, and investigating fiber coatings.
Prototype components fabricated using the additive manufacturing processes include inlet guide vanes, compressor blades, turbine nozzle segments, and acoustic liners.
Mechanical property testing and component testing in relevant operating conditions were used to evaluate the performance of the additive manufactured parts.
Additive manufacturing enabled the fabrication of complex acoustic liner geometries with integrated perforations and honeycomb structures in a single step.
Engine system analysis and modeling tools were used to assess the impact of the advanced materials and manufacturing technologies on engine performance, weight, and aircraft fuel burn and emissions.

The key factors enabling the development of the fully non-metallic gas turbine engine design were advancements in additive manufacturing, high-temperature composite materials, and the ability to fabricate complex engine components.
The researchers identified several areas for further optimization of the additive manufacturing processes, including powder optimization, alternate densification approaches, and fiber coatings.
The fabrication of the first CMC turbine engine components by additive manufacturing, including nozzle segments and cooled doublet nozzle sections, was a significant accomplishment.
The use of chopped fiber reinforcement in the ceramic matrix composites, with 20% fiber loading, was a key aspect of the additive manufacturing approach.

The researchers utilized a range of characterization techniques, including optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy, to analyze the microstructure and properties of the additive manufactured materials.
